content: Accurate and reliable measurement of CD4+ T lymphocytes (CD4+ T cells) is critical for evaluating the immune system and managing the healthcare of individuals infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The progression of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is primarily due to the depletion of CD4+ T cells, which express the CD4 receptor. A progressive decline in CD4+ T cell counts is associated with an increased risk of severe HIV-related disease and a poor prognosis. The Public Health Service (PHS) recommends monitoring CD4+ T cell levels every 3–6 months in all individuals infected with HIV. These measurements are used to determine when to initiate prophylaxis for opportunistic infections, such as Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, and to guide the initiation and monitoring of antiretroviral therapy. CD4+ T cell levels are also used to classify HIV-related clinical conditions according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) classification system for HIV infection and AIDS surveillance. Single-platform technology (SPT) has been developed to measure both absolute and percentage values of lymphocyte subsets using a single tube. Previously, absolute T cell counts were derived using dual-platform technology, which required three separate measurements from two instruments: a hematology analyzer and a flow cytometer. The CD4+ T cell count was calculated as the product of the white blood cell count, the percentage of white blood cells that are lymphocytes, and the percentage of lymphocytes that are CD4+ T cells. In 1997, the CDC published guidelines addressing concerns related to dual-platform technology, which remain relevant for laboratories using this method. In November 2001, a national conference on CD4+ immunophenotyping was held to discuss advances in reagents, instrumentation, and software since the publication of the 1997 guidelines. The conference included representatives from public health, private, and academic laboratories, as well as manufacturers. The resulting guidelines reflect a consensus from the conference and focus on the performance of SPT. Advances in knowledge and experience with new approaches to CD4+ T cell enumeration have driven the development of these guidelines. A gating strategy using CD45 fluorescence and side-scatter characteristics is now the preferred method for accurately identifying lymphocytes. Additionally, threeor four-color flow cytometry has been shown to be superior to two-color methods for measuring CD4+ and CD8+ T cell counts. The availability of FDA-approved commercial microfluorosphere counting reagents for SPT has reduced inter-laboratory variability, making SPT the preferred method in an increasing number of laboratories. Laboratory safety practices must be strictly followed when processing and analyzing specimens. Universal precautions should be used with all specimens, including wearing laboratory coats and gloves, avoiding mouth pipetting, and properly disposing of needles and syringes. Specimens should be processed in biological safety cabinets, and centrifugation should be performed in safety carriers. After handling specimens, gloves should be removed, and hands should be washed thoroughly. Flow cytometers should be disinfected according to the manufacturer’s recommendations to minimize biohazard risks. Specimen integrity is crucial for accurate results. Upon arrival, specimens should be inspected for abnormalities such as hemolysis, freezing, or clotting. Specimens should be processed within 48 hours (preferably) but no later than 72 hours after collection. Proper mixing, accurate pipetting, and adherence to staining protocols are essential. Stained samples should be stored in the dark and refrigerated until flow cytometric analysis, ideally within 24 hours. SPT requires precise measurement of blood and bead volumes, and reverse pipetting techniques are recommended for optimal accuracy. Laboratories should regularly evaluate pipetting accuracy and maintain records for quality assurance. Calibration and maintenance of pipettes should follow the manufacturer’s instructions. When adopting a new SPT method, laboratories should perform parallel testing with the current and new methods to identify systematic differences. Statistical tools, such as linear regression and bias scatter plots, can help assess the correlation between methods and identify potential sources of error. Laboratories should confirm or redefine normal ranges and monitor the correlation between test results and clinical data to ensure reliable performance. Approximately 6 million CD4+ T cell measurements are performed annually in the United States using either multi-platform technology or SPT. SPT, introduced for clinical use in 1996, has gained widespread adoption due to its technical simplicity and improved accuracy. Studies have demonstrated the benefits of SPT, including increased confidence in results, reproducibility, and reduced biohazard risks. The CDC’s guidelines for SPT aim to improve laboratory practices while allowing flexibility for technological advancements. However, measuring the outcomes associated with guideline implementation is challenging due to the lack of evaluation protocols and variability in laboratory practices. Future guidelines should harmonize all methods that meet performance standards to ensure consistent high-quality testing.
